summary:
Travel documents are the sharpest exposure for a trans visitor to the United States. Since January 2025, Executive Order 14168 requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth. The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth, so new passport applications are issued only as M or F according to the supporting documents submitted, while passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court recently allowed the State Department to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports.

Entry carries a second, distinct exposure. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025, titled 'Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports', was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the United States to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas, with applicants flagged internally under the code 'SWS25'. The same announcement states that an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently.

Checkpoint screening risks involuntary disclosure. The National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can expose a traveller's trans status to TSA officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request a screening of the type matching one's presentation.

South Carolina's facility ban, enacted in 2024, now reaches campuses. Governor Henry McMaster signed House Bill 4756 into law on 15 May 2026, requiring transgender students in South Carolina public schools, colleges and universities to use restrooms matching their sex assigned at birth. The Senate amended the bill before passage, and the ACLU of South Carolina issued a response on 18 May 2026 framing the measure as discrimination against trans students in K-12 and higher education.

Restriction also reaches people in state custody. Reporting by Metro Weekly of 11 July 2026, drawing on the Transitics tracker, records South Carolina as one of four states, alongside Tennessee, Arkansas and Utah, holding 'freeze-frame' policies that restrict the treatments transgender inmates may receive while incarcerated. That documentation establishes an in-prison treatment restriction. The article records no South Carolina case or ruling on cell placement, special units, or solitary or segregation for trans prisoners.
tangentialFactors:
South Carolina's expansion is one data point in a wider pattern. State bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings are in force in nine states and one territory, with additional states imposing outright bans on facility use according to gender identity, and in some jurisdictions trans bathroom use is a criminal offence in certain circumstances. Twenty-nine states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban.

Enforcement is not theoretical. In April 2025 a trans student who announced 'I am here to break the law' and used a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol was arrested and handcuffed, in what civil-rights attorneys identified as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law.

The July 2026 anti-trans national legal risk assessment rates states on adult and youth law severity by reading bills. It calls out South Carolina specifically for adding campus settings to its pre-existing restriction, placing the state among the escalating group rather than in the harshest tier. The same assessment identifies Idaho as the latest state flagged do-not-travel for trans people, bringing the total to four states so designated, and records that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights alongside the federal measures driving nationwide trends.

Identity documents vary sharply by state. Kansas has enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not bear sex assigned at birth and barring trans residents from changing those markers; rights groups describe the Kansas statute as a template other legislatures are following, with further targeting bills pending. The Movement Advancement Project's identity-document map sets out, state by state, which jurisdictions permit gender-marker changes on licences and birth certificates and under what conditions.

Foreign governments have responded publicly. Following the federal document and data rules, multiple countries issued advisories warning their trans citizens about travelling to the United States. At least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the country, and those advisories followed detentions of European citizens over visa issues.
localsOnly:
Residents of South Carolina, including students, are subject to the restroom requirement signed on 15 May 2026. House Bill 4756 applies across public schools, colleges and universities and ties facility use to sex assigned at birth, and the ACLU of South Carolina has stated publicly that it treats the measure as discrimination affecting trans students in both K-12 and higher education.

In state custody, South Carolina is one of four states, with Tennessee, Arkansas and Utah, operating 'freeze-frame' policies that fix the treatments transgender inmates may receive while incarcerated, as recorded by the Transitics tracker and reported on 11 July 2026. This is a restriction on treatment, distinct from rules governing housing placement.

The July 2026 national legal risk assessment ranks states by reading the adult and youth bills before legislatures, so a resident's exposure is read from statutory text as enacted or advanced rather than from enforcement records. South Carolina's campus expansion is scored as an escalation within that rubric.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no sourced statement of South Carolina's rules for changing gender markers on driver's licences or birth certificates. Whether marker changes are permitted, restricted or barred in South Carolina is unresolved here; the Movement Advancement Project's state-by-state map is the named starting point but its South Carolina entry is not reproduced in the sources supplied.

Which specific treatments the South Carolina 'freeze-frame' policy freezes, and when that policy took effect, is not stated in the sources supplied. The documentation available establishes that a restriction exists as of July 2026, not its scope or commencement date.

No South Carolina case or ruling on cell placement, special units, solitary confinement or segregation for transgender prisoners appears in the sources supplied. Whether such litigation exists in the state remains unresolved and should not be read either way from the absence of a case in this inventory.

The July 2026 assessment is described as ranking states by bill severity. Enforcement data for South Carolina's campus restroom law, and whether House Bill 4756 has been challenged in court since 15 May 2026, are not covered by the sources supplied.
